story: Hindi film song drew on Ramleela, nautanki, tamasha and the Parsi theatre. Its lyrics leaned on Urdu poetry and the ghazal. Ardeshir Irani's Alam Ara (1931), the first Indian sound film, had seven songs. It was shot at Jyoti Studios in Bombay. Its "De De Khuda Ke Naam Pe Pyaare", sung by Wazir Muhammad Khan, is counted as the first song of Hindi cinema. Irani said he had only a pump organ and a tabla player. Singers at first recorded twice, once during the shoot and again in the studio. In 1935 Raichand Boral introduced playback singing to Hindi film in Dhoop Chhaon. Its song "Main Khush Hona Chahun" was sung by a women's chorus led by Parul Ghosh. From 1934 film songs were issued on gramophone records and later played on radio. From 1948 the music director Ghulam Haider trained the singer Lata Mangeshkar. She and her sister Asha Bhosle became two of India's most prolific playback singers. Cheap cassettes carried the songs across Asia and the diaspora until that industry crashed in 2000.

disagreements: Tree: the record's principal parent is hindustani. The English article names theatre sources (Ramleela, nautanki, tamasha, Parsi theatre) and "derive their inspiration from both classical and modern sources" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi_film_music?action=raw), but does not name Hindustani classical music specifically; Parsi theatre is not on the tree as a parent.

Origin: the record says Mumbai. Alam Ara was shot in Bombay (quote in sentence 4), but playback singing came from New Theatres, a Calcutta studio, in Dhoop Chhaon (1935) (Raichand Boral article). The Calcutta location of New Theatres is not stated in the quotes used, so the story does not say it.
notes: English 'Filmi' redirects to 'Hindi film music'; URLs use the target title. Sentence 5: Wazir Muhammad Khan's name and the song title are in the same table row as the quoted note in the 'Alam Ara' raw text, not in the quoted string itself. Sentence 9's song title 'Main Khush Hona Chahun' is in the same sentence of the Raichand Boral article as the quote. The record's 'Mumbai' and the article's 'Bombay' are the same city.
